en: The active Mayon Volcano has a six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone, so people must stay outside this area to avoid lethal pyroclastic flows.
Because the Philippines faces the Pacific typhoon belt, coastal communities in Eastern Visayas must always prepare emergency go-bags for frequent tropical cyclones.
The Valley Fault System runs directly through Metro Manila, so residents must secure heavy furniture to prevent injuries during strong earthquakes.
Avoid swimming in the polluted waters of the Pasig River to prevent contracting leptospirosis, a serious bacterial infection spread by rat urine.
Due to the tropical climate near the equator, students in the Philippines must drink plenty of water to prevent dangerous heat exhaustion.
The warm, humid climate of Palawan allows mosquitoes to breed year-round, so removing stagnant water around your house prevents dengue fever.
When hiking Mount Pulag, wearing thick jackets is necessary to prevent hypothermia from the freezing sub-zero temperatures at the highest peak.
The strong ocean currents around Verde Island Passage in Batangas can sweep swimmers away, so always wear a life jacket when boating.
Heavy monsoon rains on the steep slopes of the Cordillera mountains increase landslide risks, so residents must evacuate when warned by authorities.
Drinking untreated water from remote springs in the Sierra Madre mountains can cause cholera, so always boil water for one minute before drinking.
When exploring the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River in Palawan, wearing a hard hat protects your head from low cave ceilings and falling rocks.
Inhaling volcanic ash from Taal Volcano can damage your lungs, so wearing an N95 mask protects your respiratory system during eruptions.
